Polynomial Depth Cueing was introduced by Marc Levoy in his 1992 paper "Volume Rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem" as an extension to handle specular reflections and non-linear depth attenuation [S1, S2, unofficial].

The evidence in Source [S1] and Source [S2] explicitly describes an extension to the Fourier projection-slice method for volume rendering. This extension involves using polynomial depth cueing (such as inverse square law falloff) and handling specular reflections (Phong model) by replacing normal and halfway vectors with depth and view vectors in polynomial expansions. The text attributes these techniques to the context of Marc Levoy's work (referencing [Levoy88] and the specific equations 3.4.1/3.4.2 which are part of the paper 'Volume Rendering using the Fourier Projection-Slice Theorem'). The claim accurately reflects the content regarding the introduction of these specific extensions within that paper.
supported

Polynomial Depth Cueing is an extension of the Fourier projection-slice volume rendering method that replaces linear attenuation with non-linear depth cues, such as inverse square law falloff, or models specular reflections using the Phong illumination model [S1, S2, unofficial].

The claim states that Polynomial Depth Cueing is an extension of the Fourier projection-slice volume rendering method that replaces linear attenuation with non-linear depth cues (like inverse square law) or models specular reflections using the Phong model. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'An extension of the Fourier projection-slice method to provide n-degree polynomial depth cueing for scenes with high depth complexity, replacing linear attenuation.' It further details that this extension can model specular reflections using the Phong illumination model (via hemispherical illumination and the halfway vector H) or non-linear depth cues like the inverse square law (by replacing N and H with D and V). Source [S2] corroborates this by describing the adaptation of the specular reflection method for non-linear depth cueing. All specific facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
supported
